I am - and have always been since I had my first computer - a programmer and a nerd. I spend 12h+ a day on a computer, 10 of which are work-related, weekdays and weekends, on a notebook or a desktop. Even though I'm just 22 I've had several health issues because of that, and here's what I've done about them. If you're just a regular nerd you might only find out about these over long term usage - or hopefully not have them at all - but here are some things you can do to avoid them.

There are of course many ways in which you can hurt yourself and many different ways you should fix it, so if you have a serious injury please consult a doctor instead of reading stuff online. This is just how I fixed what I had and I'm sharing in the hopes it might be useful for someone else.

1 - My tendons hurt!

This is probably the most common injury that arises from overuse of input devices. At first I thought the keyboard was to blame, but a simple test showed otherwise - I'm ambidextrous, so I simply switched to using the mouse with the other hand and bam! The pain was gone. Of course I could regularly switch between hands but that's burdensome, so what I did instead was reduce my mouse usage to a bare minimum - I don't even have a mouse at work, just at home. For me as a programmer it was relatively easy, but for someone not using command line interfaces and the such as work tools (instead using user interfaces which require mouse clicking) switching hands might be an option.

2- My tendons hurt (again)!

So after a few months of the aforementioned switch, my tendons start hurting again. Surely it had to be the keyboard. I switched from my old rubber dome keyboard (the standard ones) to a mechanical one with the softest key type I could find. Voilà, my pain was gone. It was expensive but a medical treatment would have been more!

3 - My wrist hurts!

The wrist should always be resting on the table. ALWAYS. If you raise your wrist from the table to type, you're doing it wrong. Learn touch typing, which is what everyone using a typing machine used to learn. Moreover, place a notebook where you rest your wrists on the table if it is too low compared to the keyboard.

4 - My shoulders hurt, my back hurts

Correcting my posture was of course the solution. This image summarizes everything you should be doing.

5 - Fucking hemorrhoids - and other circulation issues

Yeah, those suck. My legs would sometimes go numb, I had hemorrhoids at 21 and frequent cramps. I've always had a healthy diet with lots of fiber and water, so I suppose lack of exercise was the issue, but even after starting an exercise routine I was only able to contain the damage, not fix it. I switched chairs to a more cushy one and again that seemed to help a bit but not fix it. What finally fixed it was getting a standing desk (actually just a high desk such that I can use the computer standing instead of sitting) at home and regularly getting up at work to walk around and get a glass of water or something. Again, expensive, again, cheaper than a medical treatment.

Hopefully this helps someone!

Hate to break it to you, but you're completely wrong on wrist position. Resting your wrists on the desk surface is a major cause of carpal tunnel syndrome. They should be raised enough so that your forearms and hands are in line and not bent.

Per WebMD:

When you type or use your mouse, try raising your forearms a little so your wrists are in a neutral position and your arms and hands can move freely. If you have arm rests on your chair, you may be able to adjust them so your forearms are parallel to the floor and your wrists are neutral. Your wrist is in a neutral position when the thumb is in line with the forearm and the wrist is bent slightly back, such as when your arm is hanging at your side. You may want to alternate between resting your wrists on the pads and raising them up. If you use a wrist pad, it's best to rest your palm or the heel of your hand on the support, rather than your wrist.
